The non-death score differential is virtually identical ($\Delta_{\text{nd}} = 2.83$ vs.\ $2.84$), and the per-task death-rate correlation remains near-perfect ($r = 0.94$). Internal and deterministic death rates shift modestly ($45.5\%$ vs.\ $42.9\%$ and $20.9\%$ vs.\ $16.3\%$, respectively), but the asymmetry and its downstream effect on routing signal are stable across seeds, confirming that death dominance is not a seed artifact.
input.new_string: A full replication with an independent environment seed (seed$=$123, $N{=}220$, 11 tasks, strictly 20 episodes per task; the primary seed$=$42 analysis uses $N{=}245$ with 20--40 episodes per task) yields DAF $= 89.7\%$, within 0.7~pp of the primary analysis ($90.4\%$). The death-asymmetry label fraction rises from $78.9\%$ (seed$=$42) to $86.5\%$ (seed$=$123), and the non-death score differential is virtually identical ($\Delta_{\text{nd}} = 2.83$ vs.\ $2.84$), with per-task death-rate correlation $r = 0.94$. Internal and deterministic death rates shift modestly ($45.5\%$ vs.\ $42.9\%$ and $20.9\%$ vs.\ $16.3\%$, respectively), but the asymmetry and its downstream effect on routing signal are stable across seeds. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits zero deaths under both seeds, remaining the sole task with score-based (rather than death-based) routing signal, further confirming that the remaining 10 tasks' signal derives almost entirely from death asymmetry. Death dominance is not a seed artifact.

\paragraph{Non-triviality of death dominance.}
Three qualitatively different interventions all fail to close the gap to deterministic-level safety (16.3\%). Retry yields only marginal reduction (40.9\% vs.\ baseline 42.9\%, ${\sim}$2~pp across three trials; Fisher exact $p > 0.6$). $10{\times}$ capability scaling reduces death rate to ${\sim}$35\% ($\Delta \approx -17$~pp). Self-correction via Reflexion achieves a comparable reduction on death-prone tasks (${\sim}$35\%, $\Delta \approx -17$~pp). That two independent mechanisms (parameter scaling and verbal self-correction) converge to nearly identical death-rate floors suggests a shared bound set by the internal strategy's lack of ground-truth state access, not by any single intervention's limitations. Death dominance is robust under all three tested interventions. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits 0\% death across all conditions, confirming that death risk is task-specific. Compounding state estimation errors across multi-step trajectories create catastrophic failures that single-axis improvements attenuate but do not eliminate. Tree search with environment feedback and frontier models remain untested. Prior tool-routing work \citep{toolformer-2023,art-2023,chameleon-2023} operates in non-interactive settings where individual tool calls are independent; in multi-step interactive environments, the finding is not that death exists but that the death-rate differential ($\delta = 26.6$~pp) and its downstream effects resist all three tested intervention axes.

The 4B router's episode-level improvement ($59.0\%$) without step-level gains ($56$--$59\%$, flat) confirms that capacity scaling captures task-type classification rather than generalizable routing features. A per-class confusion matrix of the 1.7B router reveals that 33\% of steps in death episodes are mispredicted as ``internal'' (routing to the LLM in precisely the situations where it dies), with internal-class precision of only 0.14. All 105 internal-strategy deaths trace to a single action pattern: \texttt{focus on [object]}. In ScienceWorld, \texttt{focus on} is the answer-submission action; the LLM systematically misuses it as a general interaction command, applying it to irrelevant targets (rooms, doors, inventory items) and thereby submitting incorrect answers that trigger the $-100$ penalty.
